summary: Jason Steger's Sydney Morning Herald roundup recommends books due out in October 2023, mixing Australian memoir, fiction, journalism and international titles. Picks include David Marr's investigation of his ancestor in the Native Police, Robyn Davidson's memoir, Charlotte Wood's novel, Michael Wolff on Murdoch, and Michael Lewis on Sam Bankman-Fried. Each entry gives the publisher, price and release date alongside a short assessment.
one_line: Jason Steger's Sydney Morning Herald guide to books worth reading in October 2023, from Australian memoirs and novels to Britney Spears and Michael Lewis.
key_facts: David Marr's Killing for Country: A Family Story (Black Inc., $32.99, October 3) investigates the Native Police and his great-great-grandfather, and he calls it "an act of atonement, of penance by storytelling".
Robyn Davidson's Unfinished Woman (Bloomsbury, $34.99, October 3) tells her life story largely avoiding the Tracks desert trip, and focuses on her mother, who took her own life at 46.
Charlotte Wood's novel Stone Yard Devotional (Allen & Unwin, $32.99, October 3) follows a woman who leaves her husband and the city for a religious community, and is written in spare prose.

Michael Wolff's The Fall: The End of the Murdoch Empire (The Bridge Street Press, $34.99) is out now and focuses on Fox News and the recently retired Rupert Murdoch; Wolff has written three books on the Trump White House.
Michael Gawenda's My Life as a Jew (Scribe, $35, October 3) begins with why he ended his long friendship with publisher Louise Adler over an essay about the so-called Israel Lobby.

Laura Jean McKay's Gunflower: Stories (Scribe, $29.99, October 3) collects stories written over 20 years, ranging from one page to 20; she won the richest writing prize in the country for The Animals in that Country.

Michael Lewis's Going Infinite: The Rise and Fall of a New Tycoon (Allen Lane, $55, October 3) covers Sam Bankman-Fried, who set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX in 2019 and was due in court on October 3.
Britney Spears's The Woman in Me (Simon & Schuster, $49.99, October 25) is said to have earned a $US15 million ($23.3 million) advance and centres on her conservatorship.
Matthew Reilly's Mr Einstein's Secretary (Macmillan, $44.99, October 17) follows Hannah Fischer, Albert Einstein's Berlin neighbour who becomes a spy and action hero between the world wars.

Chris Hammer's The Seven (Allen & Unwin, $32.99, October 3) brings back Nell Buchanan and Ivan Lucie in a murder case involving one of seven families ruling the Yuwonderie district; his first crime novel, Scrublands, was published five years ago.
Aisha Dow and Melissa Cunningham's Life as We Knew it (Scribe, $35, October 3) recounts the pandemic's effect on Australia, published days after Daniel Andrews left office.
